source_batch.unit_label: Module B unit 5 (courseware unit 14), part 1: performance appraisal (objectives, uses, process, methods, errors), performance review and feedback, counselling

facts.statement: Performance of employees is the key to the success of any organisation, and the main purpose of HRD is to create an atmosphere in which employees contribute their best; their performance is therefore measured so that what they have contributed is known. Flippo (as quoted) says no company has a choice whether to appraise: it is inevitable that the performance of the hired person will be evaluated by someone, and the choice is one of methods: casual, unsystematic and haphazard appraisal; traditional and systematic measurement of employee characteristics and contribution; or mutual goal setting, that is Management by Objectives (MBO). Performance appraisal is a process by which management finds out how effective it has been in hiring and placing employees; it is a systematic evaluation of the work performed by employees, in which actual performance and the personality of the employee are compared with predefined standards (work knowledge, work performance, work attitude, leadership quality, team player behaviour, consistency, decision-making abilities and skills). It is also known as an annual review or performance evaluation.

Definitions reported by the courseware: Heyel: a process of evaluating the performance and qualifications of employees in terms of the requirements of the job, for the purposes of administration including placement, selection for promotions, financial rewards and other actions requiring differential treatment among the members of a group. Monappa and Mirza Saiyadain: a systematic evaluation of personnel by supervisors or others familiar with their performance, because employers want to know about employee performance and employees want to know their position. Performance appraisal is an important tool by which the organisation reviews performance, takes corrective steps through training, interventions or placement decisions, rewards good performance and tries to take performance to a higher level. An informal appraisal is possible in a very small organisation but is not scientific; as the organisation grows there is need for a record of achievements or failures, which emphasises a systematic appraisal system.

McGregor observed that a performance appraisal plan can meet three needs: judgemental (salary increases, transfers, promotions), developmental (telling the employee how he is doing and suggesting changes in skills, attitudes and behaviour) and counselling by the superior (giving feedback and understanding problems of poor performance); many experts consider that it serves two needs, judgemental and developmental, with counselling a part of the developmental need. The specific objectives listed by the courseware are: to maintain an inventory of the quality and skills of people and identify and meet their training needs; to motivate high-performing employees; to counsel employees who do not meet standards, helping them come up with an action plan; to determine performance-linked increments and provide data for promotions and transfers; and to maintain individual and group development by sharing with employees their standard of observed performance and helping them reach benchmarks by skill upgradation. The overall objective is to improve the efficiency of the organisation.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 309-310, Objectives of Performance Appraisal System

facts.statement: Uses of appraisal listed by the courseware: it rates all employees in a unified manner using the same rating scales, so they are comparable on a common footing; it provides information critical in deciding promotion, pay increases, transfers and training; it provides information on areas of weakness so that corrective steps can be initiated; it improves the quality of supervision because the supervisor becomes a keen observer; and, if implemented with openness and trust, it ensures better interpersonal relations between employee and supervisor. In practice the system is generally criticised by employees because it fails to meet one or other of these objectives.
facts.locator: Printed p. 310, Uses of Performance Appraisal

facts.statement: The performance appraisal process has six steps: (1) the organisation sets performance standards in advance, which should be clear, realistic and measurable, involving line managers; (2) the standards are communicated to the employees; (3) performance is measured through data available with the department, personal observation and feedback from the appraisee; (4) performance is compared with the benchmark or standard already established, and deviations and their reasons are noted; (5) the result is discussed with the employee, emphasising strong points and counselling on weak points; and (6) corrective measures are initiated and action taken on positive performance by deciding on incentives such as increments, promotions and training needed. Few organisations follow all stages seriously; difficulty in setting standards arises where jobs consist of sets of steps or actions that cannot be easily quantified, and if the stages are neglected the tool loses credibility and employees lose faith in it.

Methods of appraisal are grouped as traditional (emphasising the rating of personality traits) and modern (emphasising results and job achievement rather than personality). Traditional methods listed: free form essay, straight ranking, comparison, grading, graphic rating scale or linear rating, forced choice description, forced distribution and group appraisal. Modern methods listed: assessment centre workshops, Management by Objectives, human asset accounting, behaviourally anchored rating scales (BARS), 360-degree appraisal and 720-degree appraisal.

Traditional methods as described: the free form essay is totally unstructured and open-ended, giving the superior absolute freedom to write about job knowledge, attitudes and development needs, but it is subjective and comparison between two employees is difficult (generally used to appraise top management). Straight ranking is the oldest and simplest, rating the relative position of each employee in order of merit, but it is difficult to compare people with varying behaviour traits. The comparison method (also factor comparison) compares each employee on selected factors such as leadership and initiative; where the number is large, the paired comparison method compares two employees at a time and ranks by how many times each was preferred. The grading method grades employees on features such as analytical ability and job knowledge on a scale such as A: outstanding, B: very good, C: average, D: below average, and is widely used. The graphic or linear rating scale measures employee characteristics and contribution (quality and quantity of work with weights) on a continuous scale; the drawback is that the rating tends to be subjective and every characteristic is assumed to be equally important for all jobs. Forced choice description and forced distribution methods force the superior to make choices to minimise bias: the employee is rated on a predetermined distribution scale or the superior selects the statements that best describe the employee. The group appraisal method has the employee rated by a group (the immediate supervisor and three or four others who know the employee's performance): a thorough method with the least bias, but time-consuming and liable to become a ritual when many employees are rated.

Management by Objectives (MBO) tries to minimise external controls and emphasises the motivation of employees through joint goal setting and participation in decisions that directly affect them; it is a result-oriented system that emphasises goal achievement over the method. The MBO process: organisational goals are first set as measurable targets, realistic and achievable though challenging; short-term performance goals are set jointly by employees and their superiors; there are frequent one-to-one reviews of performance; and feedback in these meetings lets goals be altered if required and motivates because the employee knows where he stands. Advantages: participative goal setting; enhanced motivation; an atmosphere of competition; an objective appraisal method; early identification of problems through reviews and feedback; and an effective tool for identifying training and development needs. Disadvantages: it concentrates on results rather than process; it may lead to unhealthy competition among employees; it may create a conflicting situation in goal setting; and sometimes very soft targets are set to show higher achievement.

Human asset accounting treats the employees of an organisation as human capital and attaches money estimates to the value of an organisation's personnel and its external goodwill, on the principle that human assets, like other assets, are valuable: if a trained and experienced employee leaves, the human asset value depreciates, and a new employee with important skills and experience raises it. The current value is assessed by periodic measurement of two variables, the key causal variable (management policies, strategies, skills) and the intervening variable (loyalty, attitudes, motivation, effective interaction); it is not a method of individual performance measurement but can measure human performance of the organisation as a whole as an increase or decrease in human asset value. Behaviourally Anchored Rating Scales (BARS) describe jobs through illustrations or critical incidents of effective and ineffective performance and use them as behaviour anchors for each performance dimension; it is reasonably objective but very time consuming. Developing BARS typically takes five steps: identify effective and ineffective job behaviours; convert them into performance dimensions; have job experts evaluate the dimensions keeping in view the job description and critical incidents; have experts rate how effectively or ineffectively each incident represents performance on the appropriate dimension; and use a subset of the incidents as behavioural anchors for each dimension.
facts.locator: Printed p. 314, Human Asset Accounting Method and BARS

facts.statement: The 360-degree method rates an employee (at the centre) through all-round feedback from people affected by the employee's performance and having adequate knowledge of it: seniors, colleagues (peers), subordinates, suppliers, customers and other stakeholders, and includes self-assessment; it serves as a feedback mechanism and, being multi-rater, is likely to minimise human bias. The courseware says the commonly used method in the service industry, including banking, has three parts: self-appraisal by the appraisee, appraisal of the performance by the reporting authority of the employee (usually including an appraisal interview and goal setting) and review by the superior of the reporting authority (to reduce subjectivity or bias); it may include both descriptive and scalar appraisal against set goals, and many banks now give feedback to officers on their performance. The 720-degree method, which the courseware describes as twice the 360-degree appraisal, performs one 360-degree appraisal, sets targets, and after a short interval gives feedback and guidance and performs a second 360-degree appraisal compared with the first, so there is a pre and post round of feedback; it is an all-round appraisal that guides the employee after the appraisal and, in its words, brings in the perspective of customers or investors as well as subordinates.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 314-316, 360 Degree and 720 Degree Appraisal Methods

facts.statement: Performance appraisal measures present performance against job-related benchmarks, but gives little light on the potential of a candidate for a higher job, because the attributes and skills needed for a higher position may be quite different (an excellent salesman need not be an excellent sales manager). Basing promotion only on the performance appraisal is a judgemental prediction, so potential appraisal is an important aspect and is to be used with performance appraisal; the Assessment Centre method used with performance appraisal is of great use, and a Potential Appraisal Report shows one form used. The traditional annual appraisal was a confidential report submitted to the head office, surrounded by mystery, with no transparency or feedback to the employee, so it had no developmental consideration and its disadvantages outweigh the positive; organisations are moving to open and transparent systems with employee involvement in goal setting, self-appraisal, regular feedback and joint corrective steps.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 316-317, Assessing Potential and Performance Appraisal vs. Confidential Report

facts.statement: Merits of appraisal: it reveals concern for performance and creates an atmosphere of openness and trust; it gives feedback to the employee and ensures corrective steps in time; and it raises motivation if implemented properly. Demerits (errors) named by the courseware: the halo effect (a tendency to let one trait influence the whole assessment, so the person is consistently rated high or low); the leniency or strictness tendency of the superior; the central tendency problem (assigning average ratings to all employees without evaluating each aspect carefully); and the tendency to compare the employee with oneself on various traits, so that people with similar characteristics are rated high. The courseware also lists, without definitions, the common errors: halo effect, horn effect, central tendency, strict rating, lenient rating, status effect, spillover effect, initial impression, latest impression (recency effect), same as me, different from me, performance factor order and sympathy effect. Appraising is an art: avoid personal liking or disliking and learn to distinguish good and not-so-good performers objectively.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 317-318, Merits/Demerits and Common Errors in Performance Appraisals

facts.statement: Characteristics of a good performance appraisal system: objective; transparent; provides timely feedback; provides opportunity for self-appraisal; identifies the potential and needs of employees; discriminates between high and low performers; perceived as an effective tool for enhancing employees' potential; and identifies impediments to low performance.
facts.locator: Printed p. 317, Characteristics of a Good Performance Appraisal System

facts.statement: Performance review is the appraisal of an employee's performance by the superior during a specified period; review at frequent intervals, giving instant feedback, taking corrective steps and ensuring results by year-end is also part of performance management, which is possible through constant review that includes the yearly appraisal. Preparation for the review: the superior gathers information before appraising (the previous year's goals, documents and reports such as statements and quarterly reports, mid-term reviews, knowledge of how the organisation or industry is performing), forms only a preliminary impression, and does not treat it as final but has an appraisal interview with the appraisee to understand his point of view. The appraisal interview is a meeting of appraiser and appraisee to get information and clarification for appraising performance, identify areas for development with training measures, agree annual targets, and give feedback on positive and negative aspects and expectations; the appraiser should be trained and prepared to receive the interview in the right spirit. Precautions: the venue should be the appraisee's place or a neutral place, not the appraiser's room; the timing should avoid disturbance; avoid getting personal (compare performance with a standard, not with other people); value the employee's opinion and encourage him to talk; do not tiptoe around (let the employee know what he is doing right or wrong and advise how to improve); adopt the role of a listener and of an encouraging senior colleague; avoid judgemental remarks that may put off the employee; and start giving feedback at an appropriate time.

Giving feedback without hurting feelings is an art: the meeting should be arranged in a congenial environment; the feedback should be objective and help the employee reach the appropriate level of performance in future; suggestive rather than judgemental and focused on training and developmental needs; the superior should take a problem-solving and not a fault-finding approach; and should never lose sight that the aim is to improve the performance of the appraisee and not to criticise him. Do: let the employee do the maximum talking; encourage him to describe his success and failure; create an atmosphere in which he opens up; use clear and actionable language; ask right and relevant questions; praise achievements; tell him honestly where he could have done well; ask what help he expects; extend all help. Do not: hold the meeting when undisturbed time is unavailable; ramble without a clear message; use highly charged language, positive or negative; allow disturbance; take a judgemental role without reasoning or evidence; criticise him for failures or non-appreciation of achievements.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 320-321, Giving Feedback and Do's and Don'ts

facts.statement: Counselling means advising the employee about his performance; in the context of performance it follows the appraisal interview and feedback when the superior concludes that performance is much below the expected level and needs immediate and major corrective action. It has been defined as an activity where one individual uses a set of skills to help another take responsibility for and manage his own work or behaviour related decision-making. The counselling process has three stages: recognising the problem or issue; helping the employee realise the problem; and managing the problem. Counselling skills: communicate the purpose at the start; be specific and descriptive; avoid commenting on the person and centre the discussion on performance issues; criticise the behaviour and not the person, without crippling; listen and try to help; offer workable solutions and act where the appraisee can initiate improvement; have no prejudice and evaluate the employee's version objectively; and successful counselling is effective listening. If key result areas or key responsibility areas are clearly defined there is less chance of falling short because of ambiguity.

Managing average performers: the organisation may try rotation, transfer, classroom training and special skill upgradation programmes; if no improvement follows, they must be handled with care, because no organisation in the Indian culture takes a drastic step of removing people just because they are average performers, though in the changing scenario of mergers and acquisitions and competition such people are at risk; humane handling is recommended, and average performers lend stability by their loyalty; the courseware says that in Indian banks many average performers survive on moderate performance because of job security and an ineffective reward and punishment system. Six strategies to turn them into productive staff: understand how they define success; find out how they think they are doing at work; assess skills and change the job role if needed; show appreciation (in public, while criticising in private); set high expectations; and motivate through counselling (motivation is an emotional need, and counselling helps remove hurdles so that the employee can perform to capability).

payload.title: Why appraise, and what appraisal is
payload.core_explanation_md:
A bank cannot decide whether to appraise its people: someone will judge their performance, formally or not. The choice is the **method** (Flippo, as quoted):

1. casual, unsystematic, haphazard appraisal;
2. traditional, systematic measurement of characteristics and contribution;
3. mutual goal setting: **Management by Objectives (MBO)**.

**Performance appraisal** is a systematic evaluation of the work employees perform, comparing actual performance and personality against **predefined standards** (work knowledge, work performance, attitude, leadership, team behaviour, consistency, decision-making, skills). It is also called annual review or performance evaluation.

Definitions the courseware reports: **Heyel** (evaluating performance and qualifications against job requirements for administration: placement, promotion, rewards, differential treatment) and **Monappa and Saiyadain** (a systematic evaluation by supervisors familiar with the performance, because employers want to know about it and employees want to know their position).

Uses for the organisation: review performance, take **corrective steps** (training, interventions, placement), **reward** good performance and lift it higher. A very small firm can appraise informally; as it grows, records of achievements and failures make a systematic system necessary.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The purpose of HRD is to create an atmosphere in which people give their best; measuring what they contributed is part of that.

self_check.prompt_text: What are the three choices of appraisal approach that Flippo describes?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Casual, unsystematic and haphazard appraisal; traditional systematic measurement of characteristics and contribution; mutual goal setting, that is MBO.

payload.title: Objectives and uses of appraisal
payload.core_explanation_md:
McGregor's three needs an appraisal can serve:

| Need | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| **Judgemental** | Salary increases, transfers, promotions |
| **Developmental** | Telling the employee how he is doing; changes in skills, attitudes, behaviour |
| **Counselling** | Feedback and understanding the causes of poor performance (often seen as part of the developmental need) |

**Specific objectives** (courseware): keep an **inventory of skills** and identify **training needs**; **motivate** high performers; **counsel** those below standard and agree an action plan; set **performance-linked increments** and give data for promotions and transfers; support individual and group development by sharing observed performance and helping people reach benchmarks.

**Uses:** rates everyone on **the same scales**, so they are comparable; informs **promotion, pay, transfer and training** decisions; shows **weaknesses** so corrective action can start; improves **supervision** (the supervisor becomes a keen observer); and, with openness and trust, improves **supervisor-employee relations**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: In practice employees often criticise the system because it falls short of one or other of these objectives, which is why design and delivery matter.

self_check.prompt_text: Which of McGregor's three needs relates to salary increases, transfers and promotions?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The judgemental need.

payload.title: The six steps of the appraisal process
payload.core_explanation_md:
1. **Set performance standards** in advance: clear, realistic and measurable, with line managers involved.
2. **Communicate** the standards to employees.
3. **Measure performance**: department data, personal observation, and feedback from the appraisee.
4. **Compare** performance with the benchmark and note the deviations and their reasons.
5. **Discuss** the result with the employee: stress strengths and counsel on weak points.
6. **Initiate corrective measures** and act on good performance: increments, promotions, training.

Few organisations follow all six seriously. Setting standards is genuinely hard where jobs consist of steps that cannot easily be quantified. If the stages are neglected, the tool **loses credibility** and employees **lose faith** in the system.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Notice the dependency: you cannot fairly compare performance with a benchmark that was never set or never communicated.

self_check.prompt_text: Which step comes immediately after performance is measured?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Comparing it with the established standard or benchmark and noting deviations and reasons.

payload.title: Traditional appraisal methods compared
payload.core_explanation_md:
Methods fall into **traditional** (rate personality traits) and **modern** (stress results and job achievement). Traditional methods:

| Method | How it works | Main drawback |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Free form essay** | Open-ended written assessment | Subjective; hard to compare; used mainly for top management |
| **Straight ranking** | Rank by merit; oldest and simplest | Hard to compare people with different behaviour traits |
| **Comparison** (paired comparison) | Compare on selected factors; pairs two at a time and count preferences | Burdensome with large numbers |
| **Grading** | Grade on features such as analytical ability: A outstanding, B very good, C average, D below average | Widely used; scale choices matter |
| **Graphic / linear rating scale** | Rate characteristics and contribution (quality and quantity, weighted) on a continuous scale | Subjective; assumes every trait equally important for all jobs |
| **Forced choice / forced distribution** | The superior must choose descriptive statements, or place employees on a set distribution | Meant to minimise bias, forces choices |
| **Group appraisal** | A group (immediate supervisor plus three or four others) rates the employee | Thorough, least bias; time consuming and may become a ritual |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Forced distribution and forced choice reduce leniency and central tendency by design, at the cost of rating some people lower than they deserve.

self_check.prompt_text: Which traditional method is the oldest and simplest?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Straight ranking.

payload.title: Management by Objectives (MBO)
payload.core_explanation_md:
MBO tries to **minimise external control** and raise motivation through **joint goal setting** and participation in decisions that affect the employee. It is **result-oriented**: goal achievement counts more than the method.

**Process:**

1. Set organisational goals as **measurable** targets: realistic and achievable, though challenging.
2. Set short-term performance goals **jointly** by employee and superior.
3. Hold **frequent one-to-one reviews**.
4. Share **feedback** in these meetings: goals can be altered if required, and the employee knows where he stands.

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- |
| Participative goal setting | Concentrates on **results, not process** |
| Higher motivation | May create **unhealthy competition** |
| An atmosphere of healthy competition | May create **conflict** in setting goals |
| An **objective** appraisal method | Sometimes **soft targets** are set to show higher achievement |
| Early identification of problems | |
| Identifies training and development needs | |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: In banks, goal setting is easiest for a branch manager, whose business parameters can be expressed in numbers; it is harder for roles whose work is qualitative.

self_check.prompt_text: Name one advantage and one disadvantage of MBO.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Advantage: participative goal setting (or objective appraisal). Disadvantage: it focuses on results rather than process, or may encourage unhealthy competition or soft targets.

payload.title: Human asset accounting and BARS
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Human asset accounting** treats people as **human capital** and attaches a money estimate to the organisation's personnel and its goodwill. If a trained, experienced employee leaves, the human asset value falls; if a skilled new employee joins, it rises. The value is assessed periodically from two variables: the **key causal variable** (management policies, strategies, skills) and the **intervening variable** (loyalty, attitudes, motivation, interaction). It is **not** a method of appraising an individual; at best it measures the human performance of the **organisation as a whole**.

**Behaviourally Anchored Rating Scales (BARS):** describe the job through **critical incidents** of effective and ineffective performance and use them as **behavioural anchors** on a rating scale. Reasonably objective but very time consuming. Five steps:

1. Identify effective and ineffective job behaviours.
2. Convert them into performance dimensions.
3. Job experts evaluate the dimensions against the job description and incidents.
4. Experts rate how effectively or ineffectively each incident represents performance on a dimension.
5. Use a subset of the incidents as behavioural anchors for each dimension.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: BARS evaluates performance in terms of critical employee behaviours, which makes ratings more specific than a plain trait scale.

self_check.prompt_text: Is human asset accounting a method for appraising an individual employee?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: it measures the human asset value of the organisation as a whole.

payload.title: 360-degree and 720-degree appraisal, and the usual bank method
payload.core_explanation_md:
**360-degree appraisal:** the employee is at the **centre** and is rated by people affected by the performance and familiar with it: **seniors, peers, subordinates, suppliers, customers** and other stakeholders, plus **self-assessment**. It gives all-round feedback and, being multi-rater, is likely to **minimise human bias**.

**The usual method in banks** (the courseware's description) has three parts:

1. **Self-appraisal** by the appraisee (a chance to assess oneself dispassionately).
2. **Appraisal by the reporting authority**, usually with an appraisal interview and goal setting.
3. **Review by the superior of the reporting authority**, to reduce subjectivity or bias.

It may combine descriptive and scale ratings against set goals. In the private sector appraisal is taken more seriously because financial rewards are linked to it.

**720-degree appraisal** (courseware): a 360-degree appraisal **done twice**. After the first, targets are set; after a short interval, feedback and guidance are given and a **second 360-degree** appraisal is compared with the first, giving a **pre- and post-round of feedback**. It is a double check that guides the employee to achieve targets.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The 720-degree label is the courseware's way of describing a repeated 360-degree cycle with feedback in between; it is not a different set of raters.

self_check.prompt_text: Who may rate an employee in a 360-degree appraisal?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Seniors, colleagues, subordinates, suppliers, customers and other stakeholders, and the employee through self-assessment.

payload.title: Potential appraisal and the confidential report
payload.core_explanation_md:
Appraisal looks at **present performance** against job benchmarks. It says little about **potential** for a higher job, because the higher job may need quite different attributes: an excellent salesman need not be an excellent sales manager. Promoting on appraisal alone is a **judgemental prediction**. So **potential appraisal** is used **with** performance appraisal (for example through a Potential Appraisal Report), and the **assessment centre** method helps.

| Confidential report (old) | Open appraisal (new) |
| --- | --- |
| Annual report sent to head office | Employee involved in goal setting |
| Surrounded by mystery; no transparency | Self-appraisal and regular feedback |
| **No feedback** to the employee | Joint corrective steps |
| Gives the superior power over the career | Developmental in intent |

The courseware concludes that the old system's disadvantages outweigh its positive features and that organisations are moving to open, transparent systems.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The classic mistake: promote the best salesman to sales manager because of top appraisal scores, and lose a good salesman while gaining a poor manager.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is performance appraisal alone not enough to decide a promotion?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It shows present performance, not whether the person has the attributes and skills for the higher post; potential appraisal is needed too.

payload.title: Appraisal errors and the marks of a good system
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Errors the courseware defines:**

| Error | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Halo effect** | One trait influences the whole assessment, so the person is rated consistently high or low |
| **Leniency / strictness** | The superior's own tendency to rate everyone high or low |
| **Central tendency** | Giving everyone **average** ratings without evaluating each aspect carefully |
| **Comparing with oneself** | People who resemble the rater are rated high |

The courseware also names thirteen common errors in a list: halo, horn, central tendency, strict rating, lenient rating, status, spillover, initial impression, latest impression (recency), same as me, different from me, performance factor order, sympathy. (The horn effect is the opposite of the halo: one weak trait drags the whole rating down. Recency means the latest events weigh too much. The others are named without definition in the courseware.)

**A good system is:** objective, transparent, gives timely feedback, allows self-appraisal, identifies potential and needs, discriminates between high and low performers, is seen as enhancing potential, and finds the impediments to low performance.

**Merits:** shows concern for performance and builds openness and trust; gives feedback so corrective steps are taken in time; raises motivation if implemented properly.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Appraising is an art: avoid personal liking or disliking, and learn to distinguish good from not-so-good performers.

self_check.prompt_text: A manager rates an employee high on every trait because of one outstanding skill. Which error?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The halo effect.

payload.title: Performance review, preparation and the appraisal interview
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Performance review** is the superior's appraisal of the employee for a period. Reviewing at **frequent intervals**, giving instant feedback and correcting course is part of **performance management**, which runs through the year, not only at year-end.

**Preparation by the superior:** gather the previous year's **goals**, reports and statements, **mid-term reviews** and an idea of how the organisation or industry is doing; form only a **preliminary** impression and **do not treat it as final**: hold an appraisal interview to hear the appraisee's view.

**The appraisal interview** gets information and clarification, identifies **development** areas with training measures, agrees **annual targets** and gives feedback on strengths, weaknesses and expectations.

**Precautions:**

- Venue: the **appraisee's place or a neutral place**, not the appraiser's room.
- Timing: free from disturbance.
- **Do not get personal**: compare performance with a standard, not with other people.
- **Value the employee's opinion**; encourage him to talk.
- **Do not tiptoe around**: say clearly what is right and wrong, and how to improve.
- Be a **listener** and an encouraging senior colleague; avoid judgemental remarks.
- Give feedback at the appropriate time.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A reviewer who fills in the form from the file alone, without an interview, risks missing the appraisee's side of events.

self_check.prompt_text: Where should the appraisal interview preferably take place?
self_check.expected_takeaway: At the appraisee's place or a neutral place, not the appraiser's own room.

payload.title: Giving feedback: do's and don'ts
payload.core_explanation_md:
Feedback should be **objective**, help the employee reach the right level next time, be **suggestive rather than judgemental**, focus on **training and development needs**, take a **problem-solving, not fault-finding** approach, and keep sight of its aim: to **improve performance**, not to criticise.

| Do | Don't |
| --- | --- |
| Let the employee do **most of the talking** | Hold the meeting when you cannot give **undisturbed time** |
| Encourage him to describe **success and failure** | Ramble without a **clear message** |
| Create an atmosphere where he **opens up** | Use **highly charged** language, positive or negative |
| Use **clear and actionable** language | Allow **disturbance** once it starts |
| Ask **relevant questions** | Take a **judgemental** role without reasons or evidence |
| **Praise** achievements | **Criticise** him for failures or for not appreciating achievements |
| Say **honestly** where he could have done better | |
| Ask **what help** he expects and give it | |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Trust is reinforced when a sincere attempt is made to help: the interview is a development tool, not an examination.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two "don'ts" of an appraisal feedback meeting.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Any two of: meeting without undisturbed time, rambling, charged language, allowing disturbance, a judgemental stance without evidence, criticising for failures.

payload.title: Counselling a low performer
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Counselling** means advising the employee about performance. It comes **after** the appraisal interview and feedback, when the superior concludes that performance is **far below** expected and needs **immediate, major** corrective action. It is defined as using a set of skills to help another person take **responsibility** for and manage his own work-related decisions.

**Three stages:**

1. **Recognise** the problem or issue.
2. **Help the employee realise** the problem.
3. **Manage** the problem.

**Skills:**

- State the **purpose** at the start.
- Be **specific and descriptive**, about performance, not about the person.
- **Criticise behaviour, not the person**, and do so without crippling.
- Offer **workable solutions** and act where the appraisee can start to improve.
- Avoid **prejudice**; weigh the employee's version objectively.

items.title: Why appraise, and what appraisal is
items.core_explanation_md:
A bank cannot decide whether to appraise its people: someone will judge their performance, formally or not. The choice is the **method** (Flippo, as quoted):

1. casual, unsystematic, haphazard appraisal;
2. traditional, systematic measurement of characteristics and contribution;
3. mutual goal setting: **Management by Objectives (MBO)**.

**Performance appraisal** is a systematic evaluation of the work employees perform, comparing actual performance and personality against **predefined standards** (work knowledge, work performance, attitude, leadership, team behaviour, consistency, decision-making, skills). It is also called annual review or performance evaluation.

Definitions the courseware reports: **Heyel** (evaluating performance and qualifications against job requirements for administration: placement, promotion, rewards, differential treatment) and **Monappa and Saiyadain** (a systematic evaluation by supervisors familiar with the performance, because employers want to know about it and employees want to know their position).

Uses for the organisation: review performance, take **corrective steps** (training, interventions, placement), **reward** good performance and lift it higher. A very small firm can appraise informally; as it grows, records of achievements and failures make a systematic system necessary.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The purpose of HRD is to create an atmosphere in which people give their best; measuring what they contributed is part of that.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Casual, unsystematic and haphazard appraisal; traditional systematic measurement of characteristics and contribution; mutual goal setting, that is MBO.

items.title: The six steps of the appraisal process
items.core_explanation_md:
1. **Set performance standards** in advance: clear, realistic and measurable, with line managers involved.
2. **Communicate** the standards to employees.
3. **Measure performance**: department data, personal observation, and feedback from the appraisee.
4. **Compare** performance with the benchmark and note the deviations and their reasons.
5. **Discuss** the result with the employee: stress strengths and counsel on weak points.
6. **Initiate corrective measures** and act on good performance: increments, promotions, training.

Few organisations follow all six seriously. Setting standards is genuinely hard where jobs consist of steps that cannot easily be quantified. If the stages are neglected, the tool **loses credibility** and employees **lose faith** in the system.

items.title: Traditional appraisal methods compared
items.core_explanation_md:
Methods fall into **traditional** (rate personality traits) and **modern** (stress results and job achievement). Traditional methods:

| Method | How it works | Main drawback |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Free form essay** | Open-ended written assessment | Subjective; hard to compare; used mainly for top management |
| **Straight ranking** | Rank by merit; oldest and simplest | Hard to compare people with different behaviour traits |
| **Comparison** (paired comparison) | Compare on selected factors; pairs two at a time and count preferences | Burdensome with large numbers |
| **Grading** | Grade on features such as analytical ability: A outstanding, B very good, C average, D below average | Widely used; scale choices matter |
| **Graphic / linear rating scale** | Rate characteristics and contribution (quality and quantity, weighted) on a continuous scale | Subjective; assumes every trait equally important for all jobs |
| **Forced choice / forced distribution** | The superior must choose descriptive statements, or place employees on a set distribution | Meant to minimise bias, forces choices |
| **Group appraisal** | A group (immediate supervisor plus three or four others) rates the employee | Thorough, least bias; time consuming and may become a ritual |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Forced distribution and forced choice reduce leniency and central tendency by design, at the cost of rating some people lower than they deserve.

items.title: Management by Objectives (MBO)
items.core_explanation_md:
MBO tries to **minimise external control** and raise motivation through **joint goal setting** and participation in decisions that affect the employee. It is **result-oriented**: goal achievement counts more than the method.

**Process:**

1. Set organisational goals as **measurable** targets: realistic and achievable, though challenging.
2. Set short-term performance goals **jointly** by employee and superior.
3. Hold **frequent one-to-one reviews**.
4. Share **feedback** in these meetings: goals can be altered if required, and the employee knows where he stands.

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- |
| Participative goal setting | Concentrates on **results, not process** |
| Higher motivation | May create **unhealthy competition** |
| An atmosphere of healthy competition | May create **conflict** in setting goals |
| An **objective** appraisal method | Sometimes **soft targets** are set to show higher achievement |
| Early identification of problems | |

items.title: Human asset accounting and BARS
items.core_explanation_md:
**Human asset accounting** treats people as **human capital** and attaches a money estimate to the organisation's personnel and its goodwill. If a trained, experienced employee leaves, the human asset value falls; if a skilled new employee joins, it rises. The value is assessed periodically from two variables: the **key causal variable** (management policies, strategies, skills) and the **intervening variable** (loyalty, attitudes, motivation, interaction). It is **not** a method of appraising an individual; at best it measures the human performance of the **organisation as a whole**.

**Behaviourally Anchored Rating Scales (BARS):** describe the job through **critical incidents** of effective and ineffective performance and use them as **behavioural anchors** on a rating scale. Reasonably objective but very time consuming. Five steps:

1. Identify effective and ineffective job behaviours.
2. Convert them into performance dimensions.
3. Job experts evaluate the dimensions against the job description and incidents.
4. Experts rate how effectively or ineffectively each incident represents performance on a dimension.
5. Use a subset of the incidents as behavioural anchors for each dimension.
items.expanded_explanation_md: BARS evaluates performance in terms of critical employee behaviours, which makes ratings more specific than a plain trait scale.

self_check.expected_takeaway: No: it measures the human asset value of the organisation as a whole.

items.title: 360-degree and 720-degree appraisal, and the usual bank method
items.core_explanation_md:
**360-degree appraisal:** the employee is at the **centre** and is rated by people affected by the performance and familiar with it: **seniors, peers, subordinates, suppliers, customers** and other stakeholders, plus **self-assessment**. It gives all-round feedback and, being multi-rater, is likely to **minimise human bias**.

**The usual method in banks** (the courseware's description) has three parts:

1. **Self-appraisal** by the appraisee (a chance to assess oneself dispassionately).
2. **Appraisal by the reporting authority**, usually with an appraisal interview and goal setting.
3. **Review by the superior of the reporting authority**, to reduce subjectivity or bias.

It may combine descriptive and scale ratings against set goals. In the private sector appraisal is taken more seriously because financial rewards are linked to it.

After the first, targets are set; after a short interval, feedback and guidance are given and a **second 360-degree** appraisal is compared with the first, giving a **pre- and post-round of feedback**. It is a double check that guides the employee to achieve targets.

items.title: Potential appraisal and the confidential report
items.core_explanation_md:
Appraisal looks at **present performance** against job benchmarks. It says little about **potential** for a higher job, because the higher job may need quite different attributes: an excellent salesman need not be an excellent sales manager. Promoting on appraisal alone is a **judgemental prediction**. So **potential appraisal** is used **with** performance appraisal (for example through a Potential Appraisal Report), and the **assessment centre** method helps.

| Confidential report (old) | Open appraisal (new) |
| --- | --- |
| Annual report sent to head office | Employee involved in goal setting |
| Surrounded by mystery; no transparency | Self-appraisal and regular feedback |
| **No feedback** to the employee | Joint corrective steps |
| Gives the superior power over the career | Developmental in intent |

The courseware concludes that the old system's disadvantages outweigh its positive features and that organisations are moving to open, transparent systems.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The classic mistake: promote the best salesman to sales manager because of top appraisal scores, and lose a good salesman while gaining a poor manager.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is performance appraisal alone not enough to decide a promotion?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It shows present performance, not whether the person has the attributes and skills for the higher post; potential appraisal is needed too.

items.title: Appraisal errors and the marks of a good system
items.core_explanation_md:
**Errors the courseware defines:**

| Error | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Halo effect** | One trait influences the whole assessment, so the person is rated consistently high or low |
| **Leniency / strictness** | The superior's own tendency to rate everyone high or low |
| **Central tendency** | Giving everyone **average** ratings without evaluating each aspect carefully |
| **Comparing with oneself** | People who resemble the rater are rated high |

The courseware also names thirteen common errors in a list: halo, horn, central tendency, strict rating, lenient rating, status, spillover, initial impression, latest impression (recency), same as me, different from me, performance factor order, sympathy. (The horn effect is the opposite of the halo: one weak trait drags the whole rating down. Recency means the latest events weigh too much. The others are named without definition in the courseware.)

**A good system is:** objective, transparent, gives timely feedback, allows self-appraisal, identifies potential and needs, discriminates between high and low performers, is seen as enhancing potential, and finds the impediments to low performance.

**Merits:** shows concern for performance and builds openness and trust; gives feedback so corrective steps are taken in time; raises motivation if implemented properly.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Appraising is an art: avoid personal liking or disliking, and learn to distinguish good from not-so-good performers.

self_check.prompt_text: A manager rates an employee high on every trait because of one outstanding skill. Which error?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The halo effect.

items.title: Performance review, preparation and the appraisal interview
items.core_explanation_md:
**Performance review** is the superior's appraisal of the employee for a period. Reviewing at **frequent intervals**, giving instant feedback and correcting course is part of **performance management**, which runs through the year, not only at year-end.

**Preparation by the superior:** gather the previous year's **goals**, reports and statements, **mid-term reviews** and an idea of how the organisation or industry is doing; form only a **preliminary** impression and **do not treat it as final**: hold an appraisal interview to hear the appraisee's view.

**The appraisal interview** gets information and clarification, identifies **development** areas with training measures, agrees **annual targets** and gives feedback on strengths, weaknesses and expectations.

**Precautions:**

- Venue: the **appraisee's place or a neutral place**, not the appraiser's room.
- Timing: free from disturbance.
- **Do not get personal**: compare performance with a standard, not with other people.
- **Value the employee's opinion**; encourage him to talk.
- **Do not tiptoe around**: say clearly what is right and wrong, and how to improve.
- Be a **listener** and an encouraging senior colleague; avoid judgemental remarks.
- Give feedback at the appropriate time.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A reviewer who fills in the form from the file alone, without an interview, risks missing the appraisee's side of events.

self_check.prompt_text: Where should the appraisal interview preferably take place?
self_check.expected_takeaway: At the appraisee's place or a neutral place, not the appraiser's own room.

items.title: Giving feedback: do's and don'ts
items.core_explanation_md:
Feedback should be **objective**, help the employee reach the right level next time, be **suggestive rather than judgemental**, focus on **training and development needs**, take a **problem-solving, not fault-finding** approach, and keep sight of its aim: to **improve performance**, not to criticise.

| Do | Don't |
| --- | --- |
| Let the employee do **most of the talking** | Hold the meeting when you cannot give **undisturbed time** |
| Encourage him to describe **success and failure** | Ramble without a **clear message** |
| Create an atmosphere where he **opens up** | Use **highly charged** language, positive or negative |
| Use **clear and actionable** language | Allow **disturbance** once it starts |
| Ask **relevant questions** | Take a **judgemental** role without reasons or evidence |
| **Praise** achievements | **Criticise** him for failures or for not appreciating achievements |
| Say **honestly** where he could have done better | |
| Ask **what help** he expects and give it | |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Trust is reinforced when a sincere attempt is made to help: the interview is a development tool, not an examination.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two "don'ts" of an appraisal feedback meeting.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Any two of: meeting without undisturbed time, rambling, charged language, allowing disturbance, a judgemental stance without evidence, criticising for failures.

items.title: Counselling a low performer
items.core_explanation_md:
**Counselling** means advising the employee about performance. It comes **after** the appraisal interview and feedback, when the superior concludes that performance is **far below** expected and needs **immediate, major** corrective action. It is defined as using a set of skills to help another person take **responsibility** for and manage his own work-related decisions.

**Three stages:**

1. **Recognise** the problem or issue.
2. **Help the employee realise** the problem.
3. **Manage** the problem.

**Skills:**

- State the **purpose** at the start.
- Be **specific and descriptive**, about performance, not about the person.
- **Criticise behaviour, not the person**, and do so without crippling.
- Offer **workable solutions** and act where the appraisee can start to improve.
- Avoid **prejudice**; weigh the employee's version objectively.
- **Successful counselling is effective listening.**

Clear key result areas lower the chance of falling short through **ambiguity**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: It is a human tendency to react negatively to feedback and counselling, so the counsellor should expect it and not take it personally.

self_check.prompt_text: What are the three stages of the counselling process?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Recognising the problem, helping the employee realise it, and managing it.

items.title: Managing average performers
items.core_explanation_md:
Every organisation has many **average performers**. They lend stability through loyalty, but their motivation is often low.

**What the courseware recommends:** try **rotation**, **transfer**, classroom training and **skill upgradation**. If these fail, handle with care and **humanely**; the courseware notes that organisations in the Indian culture rarely remove people just for being average, although mergers and competition put them at risk. It observes that in Indian banks many average performers stay on moderate performance because of **job security** and an **ineffective reward and punishment system**.

**Six strategies:**

| Strategy | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| Understand how they define success | Outside interests and what sparks enthusiasm |
| Find out how they think they are doing | They may not know they are only average |
| Assess skills; **change the job role** | Lateral moves can spur them |
| **Show appreciation** | Praise in public, criticise in private |
| **Set high expectations** | Move the bar a little each time |
| **Motivate through counselling** | Motivation is an emotional need; counselling removes hurdles |
items.expanded_explanation_md: If the cause of average performance is attitude, counselling can address it; if it is a skill gap, training or a role change fits better.

self_check.prompt_text: Which rule does the courseware attach to showing appreciation to average performers?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Appreciate in public and criticise (or depreciate) in private.
